name: Jade Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say to others and what you think privately. What is a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Jade, 43, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes vehicle-inspection software. I have a bachelor’s degree and can handle most normal fixes, though the difficult rules go to our specialist. I read failed inspection reports, check the code that sent them, and speak to a garage when the numbers do not match. I have never used an AI tool; I like being able to show each step of a correction.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What depends on that income at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Ben, drives a delivery van, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is low for a developer, our savings would not cover a month, and there are few similar jobs nearby. Ben’s older van needs regular repairs, so we decide each month what can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the garage team AI Plateau still leaves us checking inspection faults ourselves. A faster form is welcome, but it cannot send a vehicle out with the wrong brake result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved that my job stays familiar. I would still be watching the mortgage and van bills because our savings do not cover even one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing failed inspection reports with garage notes and ask the specialist to check unusual brake rules. I’d put 20 into a van-repair envelope after payday if Ben gets his usual routes. In the first year I’d ask for a written date on the pay review my manager postponed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary bills, even with little change from AI. The delivery van can take a week’s spare money in one morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which purchase would come first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay for safe tyres before replacing our kitchen table. Ben needs the van for his routes, and the old table still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the delayed pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my manager the inspection errors I found before release and ask when the review will happen. I would not count a raise before it appears on a payslip.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking inspection faults.
I would keep **brake results** under human review before a vehicle leaves.
think: I feel **relieved** my familiar work remains.
I still fear **mortgage and van bills** with less than a month saved.
do: **Keep** comparing garage notes with reports and specialist-checking unusual rules.
**Set aside** 20 for van repairs when Ben’s routes hold.
**Request** a pay-review date and defer the kitchen table until safe van tyres are paid.
feel: **Anxious** about bills despite steady work in this picture.
S0.quote: The delivery van can take a week’s spare money in one morning.
fieldNote: Her **baseline money worry** comes from the mortgage and van upkeep rather than AI.
The **20 transfer** depends on Ben’s routes; she will not count a raise before receiving it.
The **table replacement** waits behind safe tyres needed for Ben’s delivery income.

steps.text: Keep checking vehicle-inspection reports against garage notes
Set aside 20 for van repairs if delivery routes hold
Defer kitchen table purchase until safe van tyres are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may let software write fixes, check results and answer garages faster. I would ask my manager which inspection failures the new checker has actually caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a smaller team could leave me out. I have never used AI tools. A manager who sees only speed may not value the garage calls I make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our specialist to run an approved AI checker on ten old brake-result faults while I compare each garage report. If it finds all ten correctly, I’d learn its review screen during paid work time. In the first year, if our hours fall, I’d cancel the children’s paid sports club and ask Ben what the van can earn without extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect my own hours could shrink, and there is not a month of money between us and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell the children about the sports club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the sports club is on hold if the hours actually fall, not because of a rumour. We could still kick a ball in the park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old case would you show management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my manager the brake case where a false pass needed a garage call. If the checker misses it, I would not sign off on faster targets.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed fixes, checks and garage replies.
I would ask which **inspection faults** the checker really catches.
think: I fear a **smaller team** could cut my hours.
I worry my **garage calls** will be hidden by a speed measure.
do: **Test** an approved checker on ten old brake faults with the specialist.
**Learn** its review screen during paid time only if all ten results match.
**Cancel** paid sports club if my hours actually fall.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely reduced hours and an exposed mortgage.
S1.quote: A manager who sees only speed may not value the garage calls I make.
fieldNote: She accepts a **narrow AI trial** only when old brake cases pass and learning happens on paid time.
Her **sports-club cut** is conditional on actual lost hours, not a forecast.

steps.text: Learn approved inspection checker during paid time only if ten faults match
Cancel children’s paid sports club only if her hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches inspection-code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on driving arrive around 2031, so Ben’s van work may face change later than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer role to end and the mortgage to rest on Ben’s routes. Our thin savings cannot bridge a long search, and there are few nearby coding jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my employer now for written severance terms and call the mortgage lender before we miss a payment. I’d cancel the kitchen-table purchase and keep cash for safe van tyres. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for real local vacancies and ask my sister whether she could watch the children during interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can name the first calls, but I cannot make a mortgage payment out of good intentions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister be able to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my sister only if she has time after her own work. I would not assume her family can pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the tyre bill ahead of furniture and school extras. A safe van is how Ben gets to the next delivery.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach inspection code before driving robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Ben’s **van work** may change later than my desk job.
think: I expect my **developer role** to end.
Our **thin savings** and few nearby jobs cannot cover a long search.
do: **Request** written severance and lender hardship terms before missing payment.
**Cancel** the kitchen-table purchase and preserve money for safe tyres.
**Apply** for actual local openings if dismissed after 2028, asking my sister for childcare only if available.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely job loss and immediate mortgage risk.
S2.quote: I cannot make a mortgage payment out of good intentions.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 code shock** from possible driving robots around 2031.
Her **sister’s childcare** requires consent and time; the lender call is an inquiry, not guaranteed aid.

steps.text: Cancel the kitchen-table purchase and fund safe van tyres
Apply for actual local vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Ask sister for interview childcare only if her work allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see which inspection jobs still need people. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031, and hands-on driving robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think my coding role may disappear. Five years gives me time to learn more of the garage process, but I cannot assume a garage will pay me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one afternoon a month with a garage inspector learning how brake results are recorded, if my manager approves the time. I’d use the free vehicle-safety manual at home and keep notes on mistakes I can now spot. In the first year after 2031, if code work ends, I’d apply for real inspection-support vacancies whose wages cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to practise than in 2028. I still count every mortgage date on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show you learned the garage process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the garage inspector to mark one report I misunderstood each month. A certificate would mean little if I cannot explain the brake result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your manager refuses the afternoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a course while our savings are this thin. If the company will not allow the afternoon, I would study the free manual and ask for feedback after work.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test what inspection work remains.
I know **2034 driving robots** come after my code changes.
think: I expect my **coding role** may disappear.
I cannot assume **garage work** will pay me after full thinking AI.
do: **Learn** brake-report checks monthly if my manager approves garage time.
**Study** the free vehicle-safety manual if paid learning time is refused.
**Apply** for actual mortgage-paying inspection-support openings if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about future work while mortgage dates continue.
S3.quote: A certificate would mean little if I cannot explain the brake result.
fieldNote: Her **five-year plan** uses garage feedback and free material rather than unaffordable tuition.
The **garage afternoon** needs manager approval; any later support role needs a real vacancy and sufficient pay.

steps.text: Learn brake-report checks if manager approves garage time or use free manual
Apply for real inspection-support jobs covering the mortgage if coding ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve inspection software and teach new staff. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; driving robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my job to hold for now, but the delayed pay review and van bills still leave us close to the edge. AGI by 2036 helps me plan, but it cannot pay this month’s tyre bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking inspection reports against garage notes and ask the specialist to review one difficult rule each month. I’d put 20 aside for van repairs only when Ben’s routes hold. In the first year after 2036, if coding work ends, I’d search actual local openings before discussing a move with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present bills, though the code change is far away. I can improve slowly without pretending the mortgage is safe by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would teaching a younger colleague look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a younger colleague to trace one inspection fault with me each month. I could teach the check I know while learning the rule I missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I would keep the same house unless an actual job offer paid enough to move. I would not uproot the children for an advert.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve inspection software.
I know **2039 driving robots** follow the earlier code shift.
think: I expect my **job** to hold for now.
I still face **low pay** and van costs despite the decade of warning.
do: **Keep** checking inspection reports and reviewing one hard rule monthly.
**Save** 20 for van repairs only when Ben’s routes hold.
**Search** actual local openings after 2036 if coding work ends.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills despite longer career time.
S4.quote: AGI by 2036 helps me plan, but it cannot pay this month’s tyre bill.
fieldNote: Her **baseline financial strain** stays visible even when AGI is a decade away.
She would **teach a younger colleague** while checking her own rules, and move only for an affordable offer.

steps.text: Keep checking inspection reports with monthly specialist review
Set aside 20 for van repairs when delivery routes hold
Search real local jobs if coding work ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my desk income could end before we have a mortgage buffer. Written severance, paid learning time and real vacancies would help. My sister might cover an interview hour, but she cannot become our income plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a brake result when a computer says the vehicle passed. The person taking a vehicle’s keys needs more than a quick green mark.

headlineQuote: The person taking a vehicle’s keys needs more than a quick green mark.
portrait: Jade is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree and average skills in vehicle-inspection software.
Her **low pay**, mortgage, two children and savings below one month make van repairs an immediate worry.
She has **never used AI** and would first test an approved checker on old brake faults with a specialist.
She seeks **family childcare** only with consent and applies only for real jobs covering the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer pay before the family builds a mortgage buffer.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning time and real local vacancies would help.
